pr_title: soc: arm: nordic_nrf: Add workaround for nrf52 anomaly 132
pr_body:
Anomaly 132 states that there is a certain window after stopping
low frequency RC clock when starting it again will fail. Even though,
zephyr has low frequency clock always on (due to system clock using
it) workaround shall be applied as anomaly applies also to system
reset when LF clock was active. If system reset occurs then if clock
is started 225us to 330us after the reset it will fail to start.

Anomaly applies to RC source only but if XTAL is used then RC is also
started to act as LF clock source until XTAL is ready. XTAL startup
time is much longer (~1ms vs 250ms). It means that without workaround
applied and when XTAL is used then if conditions are met then system
clock will be available after 250 ms. As application may not expect that
workaround is applied for both sources.

Workaround mechanism requires that startup time is measured. Systick is
used for that (so far not used on nrf52 series). It is started just
after the reset and clock_control driver checks if it is running and
if startup time is within specied window then LF clock starting is
delayed. Workaround is applied only if software reset occured.

Fixes #21493.

Signed-off-by: Krzysztof Chruscinski <krzysztof.chruscinski@nordicsemi.no>
pr_comments:
**All checks passed.**



*Tip: The bot edits this comment instead of posting a new one, so you can check the comment's history to see earlier messages.*

Note that Anomaly 132 is quite scary. If Software Reset occurs then user has not much control when clock will be started. It is done in `PRE_KERNEL_2` when system clock is started. If window is hit LF RC will not start, there is no system clock and application is basically dead.

Workaround has still some weaknesses. It relies on reading reset reason. Currently kernel is probably not touching reset reason at all and leaves it to the application. It may happen that bootloader cleans reset reason and workaround will never be applied.
Additionally, there is anomaly 136. Because of that anomaly MDK is cleaning all reset reasons if pin reset reason is set. In order to be able to use workaround it is cleaning pin reset reason but this is potentially wrong if application wants to detect pin reset.

@pabigot 
> Note that applications may rely on access to the true set of reset reasons

Yes, I'm aware of that and i actually also not convinced about this solution but it shows that reset reason manager is needed since there can be multiple clients, not to mention bootloader.

> From my experience no bits in RESETREAS are preserved across a reset

They are preserved :
https://infocenter.nordicsemi.com/topic/com.nordic.infocenter.nrf52832.ps.v1.1/power.html?cp=4_2_0_17_8_2#register.RESETREAS

But on the other hand, due to anomaly 136 they are cleared if pin reset is cleared;
https://github.com/NordicSemiconductor/nrfx/blob/9136253e271f978a8da735864fc50d60e0ed68c6/mdk/system_nrf52.c#L149

>  I'm also pretty concerned about co-opting SysTick for this,

applying workaround should be optional (enabled by default). Something must count time since reset, it could be TIMER peripheral as alternative.

> > I'm also pretty concerned about co-opting SysTick for this,
> 
> applying workaround should be optional (enabled by default). Something must count time since reset, it could be TIMER peripheral as alternative.

I would actually favor TIMER instead of SysTick, as SysTick may be the system timer base, itself.

> I would actually favor TIMER instead of SysTick, as SysTick may be the system timer base, itself.

I've seen cases when all TIMERs where used in the system by the application. LF Clock is requested for the first time in `PRE_KERNEL_2` by `sys_clock` driver so TIMER would need to be dedicated. On the other hand in low power application systick won't be used.

TIMER is not used as system time in NRF52-based builds. And even if the application uses all TIMER instances, are you sure that they need to be initialized in PRE_KERNEL stage? Application initializes their devices in POST_KERNEL, so I think TIMER can be temporarily used in PRE_KERNEL_2

But SysTick may well be the selected system timer in nRF52 builds. If you still have strong reasons to base your solution on the SysTick, you need to make sure this applies only when the SysTick is not the selected system timer.

Think also that doing things inside platform_init is dangerous; interrupts are enabled, memory, and SoC are not initialized properly.

I misremembered the RESETREAS behavior; in nrfcxx the persistence is hidden as I capture the value, process it, and clear the register in system initialization.

My other point was that it seems this anomaly will occur whenever the LFRC is stopped, not just on a soft reset, so I think it should be implemented in the clock on/off infrastructure.  LFRC startup is about 600 us (and LFXO is 250 ms) so that should be asynchronous, but I believe it's reasonable to have the stop operation busy-wait until `LFCLKSTAT` confirms the stop, which should be a much shorter delay.

Also if the workaround is not attempted until LFCLK is started then the minimum delay of 138 us may be satisfied automatically with things like clearing BSS and copying static memory, and we don't have to special-case the first start.

@pabigot 
> My other point was that it seems this anomaly will occur whenever the LFRC is stopped, not just on a soft reset

Currently, zephyr starts LF clock and never stops it so reset is the only case when anomaly can be observed.  Stopping LFRC takes ~180us so it's quite a long time to busy wait. There is however a case, if systick is used as system timer then lf clock might be turn on and turn off. I will take a look how clock control could ensure that window.

> Also if the workaround is not attempted until LFCLK is started then the minimum delay of 138 us may be satisfied automatically with things like clearing BSS and copying static memory

In hello_world sample i had to add additional delay before starting LFRC (which happens in post_kernel) to hit that window.

@ioannisg 
 > if the application uses all TIMER instances, are you sure that they need to be initialized in PRE_KERNEL stage?

currently counter driver is set to initialize in PRE_KERNEL_1 (which is probably too early) but if someone has module or device initialized in post kernel and it is using counter device then counter device will be initialized in post kernel.

Another option is to use `CYCCNT` in DWT but then without driver we don't know if there is another user so ideally there would need to me a minimal driver with reference counter.

> Think also that doing things inside platform_init is dangerous; interrupts are enabled, memory, and SoC are not initialized properly.

i need to measure time since reset most precisely so the sooner the better, One advantage of systick is that it's very simple to start (same would be for cyccnt).

> I misremembered the RESETREAS behavior; in nrfcxx the persistence is hidden as I capture the value, process it, and clear the register in system initialization.

We should have a mechanism in zephyr that will read and clear reset reason on start and application access through that api. however, bootloader should probably be treated differently: not clear or set RESETREAS before jumping to application. I don't know mcuboot so have no idea if it is doing something around reset reason.
Create #22254 with simpler solution for now.

issue_context.title: System tick is not running
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
From time to time I observe the following issue on my Zephyr device:
Timestamps for logs are not increasing and application is not running.
It looks like the system tick is not working.

**To Reproduce**
Issue replicated rarely when device is connected via JLink.
I replicated it with two nrf52832 based devices (both use custom boards).
The boards are in use for longer period of time and the issue was not replicated before in similar test conditions.

**Impact**
When this occurrs, the device is unusable.

I replicated the problem again with: b413223a66ed9e857c67ee21d1e8be4768804dd1
The test conditions were the same as before.

I used debugger and noticed that `z_clock_driver_init` is called, but I did not observe `rtc1_nrf_isr` being called.

Rebooting the device using JLink did not solve the issue.
After powering whole board on and off, everything stated working fine.
@MarekPieta is it also a custom board (same one?)? Maybe LF XTAL is not starting properly?
I replicated the issue on two various custom boards.

review_comments: Where are you getting these values, and this description?  nRF52832_Rev_2_Errata_v1.2 says the window is `[66, 138] us`, and the window is offset from the last time LRFC oscillator is stopped rather than a soft reset.

Values taken from test. window `[66.138]` is related to the moment when clock got stopped reported only by `LFCLKSTAT` and there is no interrupt for that so it is quite impractical to use since you could only relate to that by polling `LFCLKSTAT`. I've reported it to anomaly authors to update that.
When soft reset ccurs lfclk is implicitly stopped so same window applies.
This bit is not cleared, so once the soft reset occurs, SysTick will be started on every consecutive reset, until the power-on or brownout one.

Note that applications may rely on access to the true set of reset reasons, so clearing this bit without providing the at-boot value somewhere will not be acceptable.

But I'm confused by @anangl's remark.  From my experience no bits in `RESETREAS` are preserved across a reset, so there should be no concern about a lingering effect on subsequent resets.

I don't entirely understand the purpose of doing this. It effectively prevents `SystemInit` from applying the workaround for anomaly 136. And below you are checking the SREQ bit, which you should, according to the errata, ignore when the RESETPIN bit is set.
SysTick might also be used by the timer driver, so you probably should use a build assertion here (or in `z_platform_init`) to check if `CONFIG_CORTEX_M_SYSTICK` is not enabled.
